title: Quantum Machine Learning for Few-Shot Impersonation Detection in Digital Account Opening
authors: Javiera Canales, Jose Ortega, Maximiliano Araya
abstract: Identity impersonation fraud may emerge only after digital account opening, requiring an early post-onboarding approach based on behavioral and transactional signals observed shortly after activation. Confirmed cases remain rare, creating extreme class imbalance and material operational risk for digital banks. We evaluate quantum machine learning (QML) against classical one-class methods in this setting using a real 2025 cohort of 3,419 digital account openings from Banco de Creditos e Inversiones (BCI), Chile, including 8 confirmed impersonation-fraud cases (0.23% prevalence). The data were provided through an industry-research collaboration between BCI and CoreDevX LABTAV under operational constraints. The best-performing configuration used only 2 qubits and was executed on CoreDevX's SpinQ Triangulum II, a 3-qubit nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) device, enabling hardware validation beyond classical simulation. The quantum one-class classifier based on Automatic Quantum Feature Mapping (AQFM) achieves 88% recall (7 of 8 frauds detected) and 9.21% precision, corresponding to approximately 70% fewer false positives than the best-performing classical baseline at comparable recall. When its 2025-calibrated decision threshold is applied unchanged to the independent 2026 cohort, AQFM detects 20 of 31 frauds (64.5% recall) with 8.81% precision and remains the best-performing model among those evaluated.
summary: This paper applies Quantum Machine Learning (QML) to detect rare identity impersonation fraud in banking data using a one-class classification approach. The authors demonstrate that their quantum model, AQFM, significantly outperforms classical methods in terms of reducing false positives while maintaining high fraud detection recall. The work validates the approach on real hardware (NMR) and shows promise for generalizing to future data cohorts.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of detecting rare, post-onboarding identity impersonation fraud in digital banking accounts, which presents an extreme few-shot, one-class learning problem.
main_result: The Quantum Machine Learning classifier (AQFM) demonstrated superior performance over classical baselines, achieving high recall and significantly fewer false positives, even when tested on an independent future dataset.
method: The study evaluates quantum one-class classifiers using Automatic Quantum Feature Mapping (AQFM) against classical methods like Isolation Forest, focusing on performance metrics like recall and precision.
model_or_system: The quantum model uses a quantum feature map implemented on a 3-qubit Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) device (SpinQ Triangulum II) for hardware validation, alongside GPU-accelerated simulation.
key_observables: Recall, Precision, F1-score, and the anomaly score $s(\mathbf{x})$ derived from the expectation value of the quantum circuit output.
important_parameters: The best performance was achieved using a small 2-qubit circuit configuration, suggesting performance is not monotonically related to qubit count.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that the legitimate data manifold can be effectively separated from anomalies using quantum feature mapping, and that the one-class paradigm is appropriate for this fraud detection task.
figures_summary: The notes reference comparisons of performance metrics (Recall, Precision, F1) across different qubit counts and between simulation and hardware results.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem context (few-shot fraud detection), proposes the QML approach (AQFM), details the methodology (training on normal data, using quantum feature maps), presents comparative results against classical methods on both 2025 and 2026 cohorts, and discusses hardware limitations.
why_interesting: The direct application of quantum algorithms (AQFM) to a real-world, highly imbalanced, and time-sensitive industrial problem (fraud detection) provides an empirical test case for quantum advantage in machine learning.
